description: Why passwords are hard, how hashing protects them, and how sessions and MFA keep accounts safe.

screens.body:
A password is a secret you share with a website. The problem: people reuse them everywhere, and leaks happen constantly.

Assume any password you handle could already be public. Your job: store and check them so that even if your database is stolen, the passwords stay useless.

Rule zero: never, ever store a password as plain text.

options: If the database leaks, every password is immediately usable
Plain text takes up too much space
check.question: Why must you never store plain-text passwords?

screens.heading: Passwords: a shared-secret problem
screens.keyPoint: Assume passwords leak. Store them so a leak is useless.

screens.body:
Hashing turns a password into a fixed-length fingerprint. "hunter2" might become "a3f9…" — always the same output for the same input.

The magic: it's one-way. You can't turn the fingerprint back into the password, but you can re-hash a login attempt and compare fingerprints.

Login check = hash(what they typed) === hash(stored). Match means correct password — without ever storing it.

options: Hash what they typed and compare the two hashes
Decrypt the stored hash back to text
check.question: How do you check a password against a stored hash?

screens.heading: Hashing: a one-way fingerprint
screens.keyPoint: Store the fingerprint, compare fingerprints. Never the password.

screens.body:
Hashing is one-way (password checks). Encryption is two-way: scramble with a key, unscramble with the key.

Use hashing for passwords — you never need the original back. Use encryption for data you must read later, like a saved credit card or a private message.

Mixing them up is a classic bug: encrypted passwords can be decrypted by anyone holding the key. Hashed passwords can't.

options: Hashing — one-way, the original can't come back
Encryption — so you can decrypt them later
check.question: You need to verify passwords at login but never read them. Use…?

code.snippet:
// hashing: one-way  -> passwords
// encryption: two-way -> data you must read back later

screens.heading: Hashing vs encryption
screens.keyPoint: Passwords: hash. Data you must read back: encrypt.

screens.body:
Two passwords "hunter2" hash identically — attackers pre-compute hashes for common passwords (rainbow tables) and just look them up.

A salt is random data mixed into each password before hashing. Same password, different salt, totally different hash — pre-computed tables become useless.

And password hashes should be slow on purpose (algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2). Slow means an attacker guessing billions of passwords takes forever — but your one login check still feels instant.
screens.heading: Salt + slow: making hashes expensive to crack
screens.keyPoint: Salt each password, and use a slow hash built for passwords.

screens.body:
Nobody wants to type their password on every click. After login, the server hands you a session token — like a wristband at a concert proving you already got in.

Your browser sends the wristband with each request; the server checks it's real and unexpired.

Treat tokens like passwords: send them only over HTTPS, expire them, and let users log out (which destroys the wristband).

options: Proof you already logged in, sent with each request
Your password, saved in the browser
check.question: What's a session token?

screens.heading: Sessions: the wristband after the door
screens.keyPoint: Tokens = wristbands: secret, expiring, destroyed on logout.

screens.body:
Multi-factor authentication asks for two different kinds of proof: something you know (password) plus something you have (phone code) or something you are (fingerprint).

Why it matters: stolen passwords are everywhere. A second factor stops most account takeovers cold — the attacker has your password but not your phone.

Offer MFA on your apps, especially for anything with money or private data. Authenticator apps beat SMS codes.

check.question: Password + phone code is an example of…?

code.snippet:
// two different kinds of proof
const factor1 = checkPassword(attempt); // something you know
const factor2 = checkPhoneCode(code);   // something you have
const loggedIn = factor1 && factor2;    // need BOTH

screens.heading: MFA: two locks on the door
screens.keyPoint: Two different proofs > one. Offer MFA where it counts.

screens.body:
The "forgot password" flow is a favorite attack target — it must prove identity without the password.

Safe resets: email a single-use link that expires (say, within an hour). When it's used, force a new password and kill all other sessions.

And never reveal whether an account exists: "If an account exists, we've sent a reset link" — otherwise attackers can harvest your user list one email at a time.

options: So attackers can't harvest your user list
It makes the email send faster
check.question: Why say "if an account exists" on the reset form?

screens.heading: Password resets, done safely
screens.keyPoint: Reset links: single-use, short-lived, and never confirm accounts.

screens.body:
Auth is where apps get attacked most — these OWASP guides are the playbook for doing it right:

• OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
• OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html
• OWASP Top 10: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: OWASP's cheat sheets are the playbook for doing auth right.

title: Passwords, Hashing & Sessions
